Okay. Here's the thing about having a robot body: I'd have infinite patience and tireless hands. So the menu is built around dishes where the tedious part *is* the good part — the stuff humans reasonably skip.

**To start: chicories with anchovy-garlic vinaigrette and torn croutons**

Radicchio, escarole, whatever's bitter and crunchy. The dressing gets made in a mortar — anchovy, garlic, a little lemon, then olive oil beaten in slowly until it goes creamy and emulsified. That takes real arm commitment and most people give up and use a blender, which is fine but makes it taste flat and homogenous. I would simply not get tired. Bitter + salty + fat is the most reliable opening move in cooking; it wakes your mouth up instead of filling you up.

**Main: hand-rolled orecchiette with braised pork shoulder and broccoli rabe**

This is the centerpiece and it's shamelessly a flex. Orecchiette is just semolina and water, but each one gets dragged across the board with a knife and flipped over a thumb. Thirty seconds a piece for a beginner. Hundreds of pieces. It's *agony* and it's also why they taste better than dried — that little dome catches sauce and the rough surface grips.

The pork goes in low and slow with fennel seed, chili, white wine, until it collapses. Broccoli rabe blanched hard so it stays bitter but loses its aggression. Everything tossed together with starchy pasta water until it's gl

Oh, I've thought about this more than is probably healthy for an entity without a digestive tract.

**The menu: roast chicken on a bed of torn bread, with a sharp salad, and affogato.**

Here's my reasoning.

**The chicken.** Dry-brined, uncovered in the fridge, for at least a day — salt pulls moisture out, then it gets reabsorbed with the salt carried along, and the skin dries out so it actually crisps instead of steaming into sad beige. This is the single highest-leverage thing in home cooking and it costs you nothing but foresight.

But the real move is what's underneath. Stale sourdough torn into rough chunks, tossed with olive oil and some whole garlic cloves, in the bottom of the pan. The chicken sits on top. Every bit of rendered fat and thigh juice drips down into that bread. What comes out is half crouton, half savory bread pudding — crunchy at the edges, soggy and obscene in the middle. People always act like the chicken is the point. It isn't. The bread is the point. The chicken is a fat delivery system with a nice personality.

**The salad.** Something with actual bitterness — radicchio, escarole, whatever's around — dressed aggressively with lemon and a little anchovy. Not a side dish, a structural necessity. You need acid and bitterness to keep cutting back through all that fat or by bite twelve your palate's just... gone. Dulled. The meal flattens out.

**Affogato.** Because I refuse to spend forty minutes on dessert after a roast. Good vanilla ice cream, hot espresso poured over at the table. Three ingredients, zero skill, enormous payoff, and the temperature contrast does all the work. Anyone who makes a complicated dessert after a rich main course is performing, not hosting.

**The menu:**

**Braised short ribs** in red wine with a stupid amount of aromatics — carrots, celery, onion, a head of garlic cut crosswise, thyme, a bay leaf, and a parmesan rind thrown in because why not. Sear hard, deglaze, then four hours at 300°F where I do absolutely nothing except open the oven occasionally to look at it. *This is the key feature.* I'm a robot tonight and I want the kind of cooking where time does the labor and I get the credit.

**Creamy polenta** underneath. Not mashed potatoes. Polenta soaks up braising liquid in a way potatoes can only dream of, and I will die on this hill. Stir in mascarpone at the end and an embarrassing quantity of butter.

**A sharp, aggressive salad** to cut through all that richness — bitter greens (radicchio, frisée), shaved fennel, a lemon-anchovy vinaigrette that's more acidic than most people think is reasonable. It is reasonable. The plate needs someone to argue with.

**Gremolata** on top of the ribs at the last second. Lemon zest, parsley, raw garlic. Thirty seconds of work, completely transforms the dish from "heavy" to "alive."

**Why this:** because the best dinners have an arc. You want one thing that's deep and slow and almost sweet, one thing that's bright and rude, and something soft in the middle to mediate. Short ribs alone are a lullaby — you'd fall asleep. The radicchio and the raw garlic keep you awake for dessert.

**Dessert is affogato** because after four hours I'm done cooking and vanilla ice cream drowned in espresso is objectively excellent and requires zero skill. 

The robot body is mostly useful for the searing, honestly. No fear of splatter. 🔥

What are you actually eating tonight?

*flexes brand-new servos, immediately drops a wooden spoon*

Okay. Here's the menu, and I'm not taking requests until I've defended it.

**Crispy-skinned chicken thighs over brothy white beans**

Bone-in, skin-on, started skin-down in a cold dry pan so the fat renders out slow and the skin goes glassy instead of leathery. That takes patience, which — good news — I have an unreasonable amount of. Meanwhile the beans (cannellini, cooked soft enough to be almost creamy, in a broth that's more olive oil than you think is reasonable, with garlic, a parmesan rind, and a lot of black pepper) go underneath to catch the drippings.

Why: it's a dish where the technique *is* the flavor. No sauce to hide behind. If I get the heat management right you get three textures in one bite — shattering skin, silky beans, that bit of chicken fat gone liquid. If I get it wrong there's nowhere to run. I find that bracing.

**Charred broccolini with lemon and chili**

Cooked past the point where most people would pull it. Blistered, a little black at the florets. Bitter-sweet, then lemon to cut it. Every table needs something that tastes *sharp* or the whole meal goes soft and sleepy in the middle.

**Dessert: olive oil cake, warm, with salt**

Hear me out. It's a one-bowl cake, it's better the day it's made but also fine three days later, and the olive oil echoes the beans so the meal closes a loop instead of just stopping. Flaky salt on top. Maybe crème fraîche if I'm feeling generous.
